fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD tells Moses, "Tell Aaron and his sons: This is how you are to bless the Israelites." (Numbers 6:23) Moses is the middleman here, and Aaron and his sons are the ones who get the words to say. The blessing itself is for the Israelites. Passing along a message without changing a word is a real skill, and I've seen people mess up a simple grocery list.

Joshua and Caleb are names you may know from other Bible stories, like Numbers 14:6, but they're not in this passage. Here the LORD tells Moses, "Tell Aaron and his sons: This is how you are to bless the Israelites." (Numbers 6:23) So the words go to Aaron and his sons. Nice try, baker, that was a strong bench of names.

Doorposts do show up elsewhere in the Bible, like Deuteronomy 6:9, but not here. In this passage God says, "Say to them…" and then gives the words of the blessing. (Numbers 6:23) Nothing in these verses tells Aaron and his sons to write anything. Good news for them, because that's a LOT of doors.

Stone tablets are a real thing in the Bible, like in Exodus 24:12, but they're not what this passage says. God tells Aaron and his sons to "Say to them…" and then gives the blessing. (Numbers 6:23) So it's spoken, not carved. I'd say no chisels needed, and my mustache is relieved on their behalf.

Not quite. The line asks that the LORD "…be gracious to you…" (Numbers 6:25) and nothing in it says stern. The shining face and the grace go together here. So this is a line about a face that shines and a LORD who is gracious, baker.

This one is the opposite of what the line says. It asks that the LORD "…cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you…" (Numbers 6:25) A shining face is not a hidden one. What the line says the LORD may be to them is gracious, baker.

That's right, baker. Aaron and his sons speak the words and put God's name on the Israelites, but God says, "…I will bless them." (Numbers 6:27) The priests are the ones who say the blessing, and God is the One who says He will bless His people.
